subject: Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?

messages.author: f207a911f8d70cb3
messages.subject: Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?
parts:
I am interesting in looking at variation in morphology of mammalian mandibular symphyses. The mammalian mandibular symphysis has few fixed landmarks that are homogenous across specimens and is mostly ovate. However I've noticed significant variation in the orientation of the symphysis, in some species the longest axis of the symphysis is close to the horizontal, whereas in others it is subvertical or vertical. However, I realized that in geomorph trying to constrain the shape of the symphysis using a Procrustes analyses would result in all of the symphyses being oriented to the same longest axis and therefore the positional information would be lost.

I thought about using an external landmark (the endpoints of the alveolar line of the molars) to define a horizontal with which the position of the symphysis would be constrained by. However, I realized that any intraspecimen variation in this feature (e.g., the length of the molar row) would be picked up as signal in the shape of the symphysis and potentially bias any analyses of shape I perform. I was wondering if there was any way to use landmarks to define a horizontal in the Procrustes analyses in geomorph, but then exclude them from subsequent analyses of shape.

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Is there a way to use two points in geomorph to only constrain the orientation of the shape, and not affect shape data?
parts:
Hi Russell,

 

Procedurally, one could use a set of additional landmarks on the mandible (or a horizontal), perform GPA, and then remove the additional non-symphysis landmarks. This will retain the orientation of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible in the set of aligned coordinates representing the symphysis (note: I’d use actual landmarks on the mandible not some arbitrary horizontal. That goes back to the days of the Frankfurt plane in anthropology which ended up having about as many challenges as it solved).

 

However, understand that when doing such things, one is no longer doing a shape analysis, and interpretation of any patterns becomes exceedingly complicated. In essence, the symphysis landmarks extracted from a larger configuration of points have a shape and now a ‘relative’ orientation; which is what your post seemed to wish to retain. However, they also do not have constant size, so there are size differences, and there are positional differences (the full configuration is centered, but that does not guarantee that the symphyses are). So in gaining the ability to retain the orientation one must now also explain which part of the observed variation is due to shape differences, size differences, orientation differences, and positional differences. Thus while procedurally possible, I don’t see this as advancing one’s explanatory power of anatomical variation.

 

I see two paths forward. One is to use additional landmarks on the rest of the mandible, perform GPA and shape analyses, but focus one’s interpretation on what is happening with respect to the symphysis. Also, adding some analyses of the symphysis relative to the rest of the mandible (e.g., PLS) might be very important in identifying whether any differences in shape/position of the symphysis are correlated with mandibular shape changes.


A second approach would be to use only the symphysis, and translate and scale them only (no standardizing of orientation). This is again technically possible, but only makes sense if the mandibles are in an absolute standard position: something we can never attain (yes, this goes back to problems with the Frankfurt plane and others and why we developed GPA in the first place).


Hope  this helps you ponder your options.


Best,


Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams
